أب: As for the first, it is the verse of Allah, Exalted: {وَفَاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا} [عبس: 31], and Abu Zayd al‑Ansari said: I have not heard the word ‘ab’ mentioned except in the Qur’an.
Al‑Khalil and Abu Zayd said: al‑ab = al‑mar‘a, by the weight of a verb.
And Ibn Durayd sang:
Our tribe is Qays and Najd, our home … and we have the father with it and the pasture
And Shibl ibn ‘Azra sang for Abu Du‘ad:
He grazes in the meadow of sorrow from his father … his villages in a hardship that accompanies
i.e. preserve.
It is said: may Allah accompany you, i.e. preserve you.
Abu Ishaq al‑Zajjaj said: al‑ab is all the clods that the walking people trample, as narrated from Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.
This is the origin, and as for the second, Al‑Khalil and Ibn Durayd said: al‑ab is a source: ‘Abba so‑and‑so to his sword: when he returns his hand to it to take it.
Al‑ab in Ibn Durayd’s statement: the dispute to the homeland, and al‑ab in their narration is the preparation for the journey.
And Al‑Khalil said alone: ‘Abba
This thing: when it is prepared and its path becomes straight, a door.
And he sang for the poor:
I have fasted and did not fasten you and like the fast … a brother who has folded a shortage and ‘abba’ for them to go
And Hisham ibn ‘Uqbah said in the door:
And ‘Abba the one of the altar the shining … his door … and a intention …
And people mentioned that the gazelle neither returns nor is known to have a rose.
They said: therefore the Arabs said about gazelles:
If she finds, then no ‘abāb
And if she lacks, then no ‘abāb
Its meaning: if she finds water that she does not tire in, and if she does not find it she does not tire seeking it.
And Allah knows best the truth of that.
And al‑ab: the intention, it is said ‘abibtu his father’, and ‘ammtu his mother’, and ‘hamamtu his uncle’, and ‘haradtu his brother’, and ‘samadtu his steadfastness’.
Al‑Rajiz said describing a wolf:
He passed a modest … of the west … and ‘abba’ my sheep and my father
i.e. he intended its intention and my intention.
أبت: Ibn al‑Sikkīt and others said: Our day becomes ‘abat’; when its heat intensifies, it is ‘abit’.
A barren place lacking rain … the sun shields it, the heat is ‘abtu’.
It is said: a day is ‘abt’ and a night is ‘abta’.
And a man ‘maʾbūt’: the heat struck him.
Abu Ali al‑Asfahānī said: ‘al‑abta’ is like a splinter of the blaze.
أبث: The Shaybani says: “al‑abith: the active, the lively.”
Amar became very active ... he eats stale meat that has been kept.
This entry is neglected by al‑Khalil, and the word is not found with Ibn Durayd.
And “al‑kabhth”: the changer of the wind.
And “al‑kabhth” is not with al‑Khalil nor with Ibn Durayd.
It is said of one who does not settle from merriment: “He is indeed al‑abith.”
أبد: They said: eternity is time, and its plural is 'abād'.
And the Arabs say: eternity is everlasting, as they say time is timeless.
The beginning is the action that remains upon eternity.
And in the speech: "These beasts have their worshipers like the worshipers of the wild."
The homes forgave their place, and their position... with a measure, the stubbornness of their speech was their division.

And Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: the 'ibid' is the product of wealth, like the mare, the horse, and the goat, because they are born every year, that is: they give birth, and it is said: the stubbornness of his face is a burden.
أبر: The friend said: the needle is known, and its seller is Abbar.
And the abr is striking a scorpion with its needle, and it stings; the abr is grafting a palm, it is said: I grafted it with a needle, and I grafted it by grafting.
The friend said: the abr is the treatment of crops by what improves them through watering and irrigation.
And the original that is like it ... the abr improves the planting of the muʾtabar.
The muʾtabar is the one who seeks that his planting be established.
The friend said: the maʾabr are the termites, one of them is miʾbar.
And that is from a saying that came to you I say ... and from the spite of enemies to you the maʾabra.
And it is said: indeed it has a miʾbar when it is a termite.
And whoever is a miʾbar with the tongue ... will cause the speech to slip or to be released.
The friend said: the needle is a large straight object with one end at the arm and the other at the fingertip.
Where the needle meets the ugly one.
And it is said: indeed the tongue's needle is its tip.
أبز: The friend said: a person 'abaz' in his enemy, rests for an hour, and sometimes goes away.
The ferra said: al‑abza and al‑qafza are two names derived from 'abaza' the horse and 'qafaza'.
Abu Amr said: Najiba is 'abuz', i.e., she endures a wondrous patience, and she has 'abazat' (she 'abaz') abzan.
Indeed I have become the mule of the son of Koz ... a mare from the womb of Abuz.
Al‑Shaybani said: al‑abz is the one who 'abaz' with its owner, i.e., he oppresses him and exposes him with it.
It is said: 'I see you 'abaz' with it.'
أبس: The black horses of Haija were not blamed for harshness.
And it is said: I harshened meaning I detained, and the thing hardened and changed.
Did you not see that the dust has become thick … the days pass over it without hardening.
And it is said: with a ya it means “he does not become despondent,” and it was mentioned in its chapter.
أبش: Ibn Durayd said: I have abashed the thing and I have humbled it: when I gather it.
أبض: Al‑‘ubḍ is eternity and its plural is ābāḍ.
In a generation we lived with that ubḍa.
And the ibāḍ is a rope used to tighten the camel’s reins to its foreleg; she says ‘I have tightened it.’
And the inner part of the camel’s knee is called al‑maʾbidh.
The diminutive of ibāḍ is ubayyid.
I say to my companion while the night is passing … I will whiten you, O master, lest it be lost.
He says: Preserve your black ibāḍ so that it does not disappear.
As if its hijāna were mutaʾabbidāt … and in the verses, the ‘aswirat al‑raghām’.
Mutaʾabbidāt: things suspended with the ubḍ.
He says as if it is in this condition and in the ropes, the ‘aswirat al‑raghām’.
أبط: I placed the thing beneath my ibṭ.
Ibn Durayd said: He ‘taʾabbaṭa’ his sword when he sheaths it, because it becomes under his ibṭ.
And everything you sheathe in the place of the sword, you have ‘taʾabbaṭtah.’
I drank from its jam and expelled it ... and a white, sharp male ibāṭī.
People said: His saying ‘ibāṭī’ means: it is the side of my ibṭ.
And others said: He is ibāṭī, he traced it to his ibṭ and then lightened it.
The metaphor: al‑ibṭ is from sand, meaning most of it breaks off and a thin, spread piece remains attached to the trunk; thus most of al‑ibṭ is broken, and the plural is al‑ābāṭ.
And Hawmāna and Raqā run their mirage ... with the smoothed al‑ābāṭ, its emergence is sharp.
أبق: The servant kept saying “I will keep (it) forever and forever,” said al‑Rajiz.
Hold your two sons, Amr, for I am … a lightning on the ground of al‑Sa‘ali, I will set it ablaze (the rest of the line is unclear).
It is said: a man named ‘Abd is called ‘Abūq and ‘Abbāq.”
Abu Zayd said: the man ta’abbqa covered himself.
But death came to him; he does not ta’abbqa.
Did not Bahani say ‘why do you ta’abbqa … you are blessed and bliss does not suit you’?
Some of them said: it is said to a man ‘you have such’, and he says ‘by God I do not ta’abbqa’, i.e., I do not deny.
And it is said to him: ‘O son of so‑and‑so’, and he says ‘I do not ta’abbqa from her’, i.e., I do not deny her.
Al‑Khalil said: al‑abq is the husk of the hemp.
Abu Ziyad said: al‑abq is a plant whose market is pounded until its seed is pure, becoming hemp.
Fuel of eight like the ashes of al‑abq.
The judgments of the pot and al‑abqa have been firmly decided.
أبل: The friend said: the camel is known.
And a camel that is ‘muʾabbala’ was made a herd after herd, and that is a characteristic specifically for camels.
And it is said of a man who has camels: ‘Aabil’.
Abu Zayd said: the word ‘camel’ is said for its foal and its young, and it has no single word, and the plural is ‘Aabaal’.
He said:
Their camels have drunk fire ... and fire cures from the sores.
Ibn al‑ʿArabī said: a man is ‘aabil’ if he owns a camel, and ‘aabil’ by the measure of a verb: if he is skilled in her breeding, and he has ‘abala’ (has become) ‘yaʾbal’.
And he is among the ‘aabil’ of people, i.e., the most skilled with camels, and they say: ‘He is aabil more than Hunayf al‑Hanātim’.
And the female camels are the camels.
And a man ‘aballa’ when his camels are many, so he is ‘muʾabbil’, and a wealth ‘muʾabbala’ in camels especially, and that is its abundance and the riding of some upon others.
And so‑and‑so does not ‘yaʾtabil’, i.e., does not rely on camels.

Abu ʿAlī al‑Aṣfahānī narrated from al‑ʿĀmirī, saying: the ‘abalah’ is like a crown for camels, meaning to treat them well, and Abu Nakhīla used to say: ‘Indeed the most rightful wealth is in the abalā and the milk, wealth that draws blood, women lust after it, and God is worshipped upon it in heaven, its milk is healing, its urine is medicine, its kingdom is splendor.’ Abu Zayd said: it is said of so‑and‑so ‘ibla’, i.e., he has a hundred camels; that was made a name for a hundred camels, like Kahnida, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “People are like a hundred camels with no rider.”
The Prophet ﷺ said: “People are like a hundred camels that have no rider.”
Al‑Farrāʾ said: it is said: so‑and‑so ‘yuʾabbil’ on so‑and‑so: if he multiplies upon him.
Its interpretation is magnification and glorification.
He said:
May Allah reward well the owner whenever he comes ... he acknowledges and does not look at the words of the ‘muʾabbil’.
He said: and from that the camels were named for their great creation.
Al‑Khalīl said: a camel is ‘aabil’ in a place that never leaves, it avoids water.
And the man ‘taʾabbala’ from the woman as the beast avoids water, and from him the hadith: ‘Taʾabbala Adam peace be upon him on his slain son for days that do not affect Hawwa.’
Labeed said:
And when I move my seed it darkens ... or two sparrows of a hostile flock have become ‘abal’.
It means a donkey that has avoided water.
It is said of it: ‘abal yaʾbil and yaʾbul urine.’
Al‑ʿAjjāj said:
As if the skins of labor are the wet ones.
Ibn al‑ʿArabī said: ‘abalt taʾabil ubla’: when it grazes on wet and dry ground – the wet part is the portion.
And Abu ʿUbayd said: camels are ‘awābil’, ‘ubbāl’, ‘uʾubbāl’, i.e., the sturdy ones.
He said:
With it she wet two months of spring, both of them
The al‑Asmāʿī said: camels that are many and wet, like they say ‘sheep that are fat’, and cows that are honored
And it is said: it is the domesticated one
Ibn al‑ʿArabī said: a she‑camel that is wet, i.e. severe
And they say ‘He has neither a hābil nor an ābil’, the hābil: the one who boasts, the ābil: the shepherd
Al‑Khalīl said in the verse of Allah: {ṭayran abābila} [Al‑Fīl: 3]: i.e. some of them follow each other, one of them is a wet one and a wet‑one
Al‑Khalīl said: al‑Abīl is among the heads of the Christians, and he is the Abīlī
Al‑ʿAʿshā said:
And what is an ābiliyy on a structure ... he built it and crucified in it and they became
He said: Abīlī wants, so when forced he added the ya, as is said: ‘aynāq and the original is anwāq.”
He said: ʿAdī said:
Indeed, by Allah I accept my pledge ... with a camel each time he prays he becomes angry
And some of them said: he wet over the dead, grieving over him
And I wet the dead like I wet
So as for the speaker’s statement:
Two tribes, from them a lazy one does not answer me ... and a ‘must‑abʿal’ from them is beaten and oppressed
It is said: he meant by ‘must‑abʿal’ the oppressed man
Al‑Farrāʾ said: the wet ones are the lowly, the single one is wet
Al‑ʿĀmirī said: he fulfilled his wetness from such, i.e. his need
He said: and it is a characteristic of evil, not of good
Abū Zayd said: it is said: ‘What do I have to you wet‑ness with a fatha on alif and kasra on ba’, i.e. a need
And it is said: I seek it with wetness, i.e. a bundle
Yaʿqūb said: a wet place
Al‑Shammākh said:
So it appeared with wetness night then night ... with a edge it turned away from their light
And it is said: the wet man ‘yābil’ (to be wet): when he overcomes and refrains
The wet ones: the weight
And in the hadith: ‘Every wealth whose zakat has been paid, its wetness has gone.’
And the ibbāla: the bundle of firewood.
أبن: A rod of Saraʾ a little al‑uban.
And so‑and‑so is called al‑uban in this way, i.e., he is blamed.
And it is mentioned in the narration
of the council of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his family: “‘Do not al‑uban in it the sanctuary’”, i.e., do not mention it.
And al‑taʾbīn: praising a man after his death.
By my life and my age I will not al‑taʾbīn a perishable … nor be distressed by what befell him and hurt him
And this is ibbān that, i.e., its time.
And you say: I built his trace: when I stood it, and I built the thing I guarded it.
The seers say to him that one is a rider … al‑ūb‑binu a person above ʿAliyā standing
أبه: What I have not known about it, i.e., I did not know its location nor have I used it, and the al‑ubbaha is majesty.
أبو: I fed the thing, its father is a father: when I feed it.
And because of that the father was called a father.
And it is said in relation to a father: my fatherly.
And a goat is ‘abāʾ’: when it suffers pain from the nostrils of the goat’s udder.
Al‑Khalil said: the father is known, and the plural is ‘abāʾ’ and ‘ubawwā’.
I avoid the region of Sham, indeed its region… the fathers of my fathers and from me its pillar.
He said: and she says: I have taken a father, as one says: I adopted a son and I mothered a mother.
It is permissible in poetry ‘these two are your father’ meaning you mean your fathers, and ‘I saw your father’ means your two fathers.
It is used for both fathers and maternal uncle.
It is permissible in the plural ‘abūna’.
And these are your father, i.e.: your fathers.
Abu Ubayd: you were not a father and indeed you denied fatherhood.
And I fathered the people, i.e.: I was a father to them.
We feed them and we raise them all… as the ropes were drawn from the abyss.
Al‑Khalil said: so‑and‑so fathers the orphan, i.e.: feeds him as a parent feeds his child.
أتب: Said al‑Asmaʿī: It is the baqira, meaning that a piece of ice is taken and split, then the woman throws it into her own neck without a pillow or a pocket.
Said Abu Zayd: I have attab the woman, I rebuke her: when I clothe her with the itb.
Said al‑Shaybānī: At‑tatub is that a man places the bow’s strap on his chest and pulls out its two ends so that the bow rests on his shoulders.
Said al‑Numayrī: The miʾtab al‑mishmal is the covered one and he has tatabahu: when he throws it under his belly and then embraces it.
And a man muʾattab of the back, and it is said: muʾtab, meaning his loins.
On a nursing hajali that is muʾattab of the back
أتل: Abu Ubayd said: the atalan (plural of atal) approach the step in anger, it is said: atal means to fight, and atan means to come.
I have seen you, I will not give you except as if ... I will ask and if you are angry you will fight.
And it is also a walking with difficulty.
What do you have, O cow, you fight us ... upon me with the smearing you are smearing.
Abu Ali al-Asfahani said: the man atal fights, he is late and delayed.
And I filled his belly until atal.
أث: Ibn Durayd said: The plant is heavy when it is abundant.
A plant is sturdy, and everything that is placed is sturdy, and it has been furnished as furnishing.
And the house’s furniture from this: it is said that one of them is a piece of furniture, and it is said that none of it is from its wording.
And al‑Rajiz said about the sturdy:
He crushes from it its sturdy plant … until you see its standing as a prostrate one.
That is, a prostrate, fallen one.
And it is said: women are furnishings: abundant in meat.
And from my desire the heavy furnishings … tilt them, their miracles the causes.
And in the furnishings al‑Thaqafi says:
The hardships have afflicted you the day they built.
With the beautiful adornment of the furniture, and thus the narration of the house appears in Mu‘jam al‑Buldan (307:8:8), but in al‑Lisan (19:8): “Bi dhi al‑ra’i.”
And the ‘ra’i’ is what the eye has not seen of a good state and apparent garment.
And al‑Mubarrid noted in al‑Kamil 377 that “Bi dhi al‑ra’i” is the correct narration.
أثن: They say that praise is the excitement of the heart.
We have stipulated in the first of our books that we should judge only the correct words.
أثوى: and I will not be for you a 'nayerab'.
and indeed a woman who ... with the support of her people ... is hot to my mind that she will be blamed and shamed.
أج: And the explanation of that is their saying: “Ajja al-ẓalīm: when he passes, Ajij and Ajj, and that is when you hear his offspring in his attack.”
And al‑ajij: Ajij of the evil one from the offspring of fire.
The poet said describing a she‑camel:
She ran and the edges of the desert were sorrowful … she moans as Ajja al‑ẓalīm al‑mufazzaʿ
And another said describing a horse:
As if the trembling of his breaths … Ajij of the reins that the north has driven.
And Ajjat al‑qawm: the offspring of their walking and the mixing of their speech, all that about Ibn Durayd.
And a people said al‑ujaj: the burning hot fire that is blazing, and it is from: the fire has flared.
And al‑ajja: the intensity of heat, it is said of it: the day became ajaj.
And the flame of the sedition is of ajaj.
And the one of the hump said in al‑ajja:
Until when the two midsummers blow for him … with an ajja that the water and moisture rose from it.
And Ubayd ibn Ayyub al‑ʿAnbari said he inherited a cousin’s son:
And I was absent and did not witness even if I had been a witness … he would have lessened from my ajij of my heart.
أح: The Kisāʾī says: In my heart there is ‘uḥāḥ’, meaning: a feeling of longing and hostility.
Ibn Durayd says: I heard someone say ‘uḥāḥan and aḥīḥan’: when he is pained by anger or sorrow.
He folds the ‘ḥayāzīm’ over ‘uḥāḥ’; ‘uḥayḥa’ is a man’s name derived from that.
It is said in the story of al‑Suʿāl: ‘aḥ‑aḥan.’
It is almost from ‘tanahnuḥ’ and ‘aḥ‑…’ narrates Suʿāl al‑Sharq al‑Abaḥ
Some of them mentioned that it is elongated: ‘āḥ.’
As if the voice of its ‘shakhbah’ is exhausted… Suʿāl, an elder of Bani al‑Julāḥ
أخ: Ibn Durayd said: “akh”: a word said when one is astonished, and I consider it a newly coined word.
It is also said: indeed “akh” is a word said when one repeats something.
And the singer’s connection was “akh” … and Dakhṭanūs was the daughter of Laqīt,

At ‘Amr ibn ‘Amr ibn ‘Udas, a great elder, he placed his head in her chamber, breathed as one breathes a sleeping person, said “akh!”, she replied “akh, by God, from you!”, and this was heard; he opened his eyes and released her, so ‘Amr ibn Ma‘bad ibn Zurara married her, and horses of Bakr ibn Wa’il coveted them, they took her, the horse chased, caught up with ‘Amr ibn ‘Amr, they pursued her until they took her, and he said while returning with her:
Which of your two husbands did you see better, the great one or the one who brings the crowd?
She said: that is in that, and this is in this.
And the ‘akhīkhah’: a thin vessel poured with water, then brightened with oil or fat and is drunk.
The old man’s vomiting concerning the ‘akhīkhah’.
أد: As for the first, it is al‑idd, which is the great matter.
God the Exalted said: {لَقَدْ جِئْتُمْ شَيْئًا إِدًّا} [مريم: 89], i.e., a great thing of disbelief.
O my nation, I rode a great matter ... I saw the two hands dismembered, guided.
White and shining the forehead, lofty ... I obtained from it a sip and coolness.
And we avoid indecency and the obscene ... and the many ’idds’ and the limbs.
It is said: the camel ’added’: when it pulls back its nostril.
And al‑idd: strength, as said by Ibn Durayd, and he sang:
I am freed from evil and I added after I was mute, guided.
Thus this is the original first meaning.
And as for the second, Ibn Durayd said: the camels ’add’ when they call.
And as for ’ud‑d of Ibn Tabkha ibn Ilyas ibn Mudarr, Ibn Durayd said: the hums in “ud‑d” with a waw, because it is from al‑wudd and was mentioned in its chapter.
أذ: Ibn Durayd said: “Azh ya’udh azhan: he cuts, like this.”
And a shafra is a’udh: a cutter.
He hurts with the blade any ... from a bundle, a safety and a ...
أر: 2. He was struck by it with a hundred links... the weight of the beetle and which zebra?
3. And the root: the burning of fire, it is said that the man burns the fire: when he sets it on fire.
4. Abu al‑Hasan Ali ibn Ibrahim al‑Qattan told us, he said: a small creature is upon us:
5. He has gone away, a traveler for a night, a path... and he has been struck or he has been tired or he has gone away.
7. As if it were a different confusion, a wandering one.
8. It began to point at it from below, its flame.

9. And the root is to treat the cow when its calf is cut off, and he is to take a branch from the thorn of a reed, then to strike it and then to leave salt on it so that its life is poured over it until it dies, it is said: a cow that is slaughtered, and that is what is treated with it is the iron.
أز: The close friend said: al‑az is the carrying of a human onto a human with gentleness and cunning.
Satan urges a person to disobedience intensely.
God says: {أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا الشَّيَاطِينَ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ تَؤُزُّهُمْ أَزًّا} [مريم: 83].
The commentators say: it disturbs them with disturbance.
Affliction and grief do not seize us, nor the enemy’s oppression, the one possessing al‑az.
Ibn al‑A‘rabi said: al‑az is the thick milk of a she‑camel.
A severe ‘az’ of the latter, as if ... when the sorcerers begin it, the caravan’s clatter.
Abu Ubaid says: al‑az means the joining of one thing to another.
Al‑Khaleel says: al‑az means a gush.
Al‑qidr, which is also al‑aziz, and in the hadith: “He used to pray and his belly was aziz like the aziz of the water‑jar from weeping.”
Abu Zayd says: al‑az is the sound of thunder; it is said: ‘azz, ya’izz, azzan, and aziz.’
Abu Hatim says: al‑aziz is a very strong cold; it is said: ‘a night of aziz’ and not ‘a day of aziz.’
He says: al‑aziz is the intensity of travel; it is said: ‘the wind azz‑ed us,’ meaning ‘it drove us.’
Ibn Durayd says: a house is azaz when it becomes full of people.
أس: They say: the root is the origin of a man, and the root is the face of time, and they say: that was on the root of time.
And the root of glory is steady and firm ... he reached the sky, his branch is long
As for the As, this is not his door, and it has been mentioned in its place.
أش: Ibn Durayd said: 'What do people do when they are angry? They act harshly toward each other for evil, not for good.'
Another said: 'The harsh ones are like the harsh ones.'
In the narration: 'When he saw some of his companions among the harsh ones, he was astonished.'
أص: The language scholars said: “al‑iṣṣ is the original.”
And it is said of the collective donkey: “aṣūṣ”.
And the plural of al‑iṣṣ, which is the original, is “āṣāṣ”.
Qilāl of glory branched ‘āṣāṣā … and ‘izzah, a hoarse one that is not to be soothed.
And al‑aṣīṣ: the root of dung in which a drink is made.
When will I see a drink around al‑aṣīṣ?
As for the other, they said: “Aflaṭ so‑and‑so has an aṣīṣ, i.e., a thunderclap.”
أض: Ibn Durayd said: He forced me to this [and that] he also forces me: when he compels me to it.
And she sees this as a necessary need, i.e., being compelled.
He said: and ‘al‑‘ad’ also means fracture or break, it is said ‘adduh’, like ‘hadduh’, the same.
And Abu Zayd narrated: ‘al‑adadah’ means necessity.
Time that I have not contradicted the ‘adadah’ ... I blacken what is white in his eye.
أط: And every voice resembling that is aṭiṭ.
The poetic line is unclear or incomplete.
He describes a camel whose belly became full.
Yatḥarun: they breathe heavily like a moan.
Al‑inā: the time of drinking in the evening.
Al‑aṭṭāṭa: the one that hears a sound.
In the hadith: “until his aṭīṭ is heard from the crowd”, meaning the gate of Paradise, and it is said: the tree aṭṭat when it bends.
The line is unclear or incomplete.
أف: Ibn Durayd said: ‘Aff’ meaning to sigh when one sighs from distress or pain, and a man who is ‘affaf’ sighs a lot.
Al-Farra' said: ‘Uff’ is a lowered sound without a n, and ‘uff’ lowered with a n; it is a sound, as sounds are lowered, and it is said: ‘taaqi’.
And among the Arabs there are those who say: ‘uff’ to him.
He said: Some Arabs said: Do not say to him ‘uff’ or ‘tuf’, as it makes it a name.
He said: The Arabs say: He would sigh from a wind he found and would sigh from intensity that afflicts him.

Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said, when Umar asked him about his brother Malik, that he used to ride the thin camel, race the slow horse, wield the crooked spear, wear the violet shawl between two bright plains in the dark night, and spend the day laughing, neither being gentle nor sighing.
Al-Khalil said: the ‘uff’ and the ‘tuff’, one is filthy of the nails, the other filthy of the ear.
‘May the curse be upon them and the sighing,’ said Ibn al‑A‘rabi: It is said: ‘uff’ to him and ‘tuff’ and ‘‘uffah’ to him and ‘tuffah’.
From this analogy: ‘al‑ya’foof’ is the iron of the heart.
The other meaning is unclear in the source; it mentions their saying about a ‘ta’iffa’ and sighs and ‘iff’, i.e., a time.
Upon ‘iff’ a migration and an hour of solitude.
أك: Ibn al‑Sikiti says: ‘Al‑akka’ means a hot, burning thing; it is said: ‘An akka has struck us from a heat,’
and this day is an akka day and a day of a person with an akka.
Ibn al‑Arabi says: ‘Al‑akka’ means bad character and a tight spirit.
When the drinker takes it, it becomes an akka… so let him keep it until he cries, his cry.
Ibn al‑Arabi says: a man comes: when his feet are struck.
In his foot from his pride, I came to you; the companion said: ‘Al‑akka’ means the severity of the most severe of times, and someone came to you from a matter that he threw away.
Ibn Dureid says: a day is akka, a day is akka, and a day is akik, and that is from the intensity of heat.
أل: The friend and Ibn Durayd said: “Al‑thing is: when it shines.”
Ibn Durayd said: The war‑cry was called ‘alla’ because of its meaning.”
And the horse ‘alla’ whines: when it is startled while walking.
And its neighs ‘alla’ when it shines in its chase.
He said:
‘Until I throw it, its neigh whines … and its sound is like the clatter of stone.’
And the man ‘alla’ in his walking: he trembles.
The friend said: the war‑cry is ‘alla’, and the plural is ‘ilal’.
He said:
‘Its ribs shine in the night … standing with war and with ‘ilal’.
And the war‑cry is also called ‘alila’ and ‘alil’.
He said:
‘He protects the shield of the sons of your father … and stabs with ‘alila’ and ‘alil’.
He said: it was called ‘alla’ because it is a fine head.”
And the man ‘alla’ with the ‘alla’, i.e.: he stabbed.”
It was said to an Arab woman who was insulted: ‘So‑and‑so sent someone to propose to you.’
She replied: ‘Hurry I will strike and crush, he has no ‘gull’ nor ‘alla’.’
He said: and the ‘ta’lil’: your distortion of the thing, like the head of a pen.”
And the ‘mu’allal’ also means ‘determined’.
It is said: a ‘mu’allala’ ear, i.e. a determined ear, said Tarafa:
‘Two ‘mu’allalat’ know the emancipation in them … like the two ears of a sheep in a single horn.’
And an ear ‘ma’lula’ and a horse ‘ma’lul’.
He said:
‘The ‘ma’lula’ of the two ears is like the blackness of the eye.’
It is said: a night ‘alil’, for a severe day.”
The mouth said:
‘With every broad‑selling youth he rises … to the caves on the night‑day.’
The friend said: and the ‘alal’ and the ‘allanan’: the two faces of the sword and the face of every wide thing.”
The knower said: and from it is said to the two matching pieces of meat between them a gap that is in the shoulder, when one is peeled from the other water flows between them: ‘allanin’.
A woman said to her neighbor: ‘Do not give your shoulder to your harm, for water runs between its ‘alalayha’, i.e. give it harm.’
As for the voice they said in his saying:
‘And he stabbed, increasing the two ‘allalin’ from it … the living girl follows it with the ringing.’
It is the story of the voice of the wailing one.”
He said: and the ‘alil’: the moan in his saying:
‘Either you will see me increase the ‘alila’.
He said Ibn Mayyada:
‘And tell her what you command with a ‘wamq’ … for him after the sleeping of the eyes is ‘alil’.
He said Ibn al‑‘Arabiyy: inside him is an ‘alil’ and a ‘saleel’.
I heard the ‘alil’ of water, i.e. its sound.”
It is said the ‘alila’ is heaviness.”
And he sang:
‘Give me the ‘alila’ if my little one is killed … give me the ‘alila’ if they are not killed.’
They said: a man ‘mi’ll’, i.e. very talkative and noisy among people.”
The knower said: the ‘al’: raising the voice by calling and weeping, it is said from it: ‘alla whines a night.’
In the hadith: ‘Your Lord is amazed at your ‘allik’ and your modesty and the speed of its answer, O you.’
They sang for the dead:
‘And you are what you are in the dark gloom … when the ‘allalayha’ the goat the noble calls.’
The third meaning: the ‘ilu’: divinity.”
Abu Bakr said when the speech of Musaylimah was mentioned:
‘This did not come from an ‘il.’”
The commentators said: the ‘il’: Allah, glorified be He twice.”
And a people said: it is a close relative.”
He said:
‘They cut off from the ‘il’ that was between us … obstinately and did not fulfill covenant nor protection.’
He said Ibn al‑‘Arabiyy: the ‘il’ is every cause between two.”
And they sang:
‘By your life, indeed your ‘il’ is in Quraysh … like the ‘il’ of the neck of a camel.’
And the ‘il’: the covenant.”
And from what deviated from these roots their saying ‘allil al‑siqa’: its scent changed.”

It may be one of three; because Ibn al‑‘Arabiyy mentioned that the one who corrupted his ‘allah’ is the one who lets water enter between the inner and the skin, Ibn Durayd said the Arabs lightened the ‘il.’
He said the ‘a‘sha:
‘White does not fear the storm nor … cuts flesh nor betrays except.’
أم: A poet said, and combined the two languages:
If mothers disgrace faces ... you have brightened the darkness with their mothers
And the shepherd said:
Their mothers and their beatings are wretched
The Arabs say: “He has no mother” in both praise and blame.
Abu Ubayda said: You were not a mother, yet you have mothered a motherhood.
So‑and‑so mothers So‑and‑so, i.e., feeds him, i.e., becomes his mother who feeds and raises him.
He said:
We mother them and we raise them all ... as the cords are drawn from the raw material
i.e., we become mothers and fathers to them.
And he sang:
Seek the father of the palm from those who refuse you ... for all of them will turn you away from your fathers
And they say: mother and nation, with the letter ه.
He said:
You accepted it from a nation for you forever ... its wine is distributed in the markets from it
Al‑Khalil said: Everything that can be added to something includes everything besides it that follows it, so the Arabs call that thing a mother.
And from that the mother of the head, which is the brain.
They say: I mothered So‑and‑so with sword and staff as a mother: when you strike him a blow that reaches the brain.
And al‑Ameem: the feared one, which is also the stone used to pierce heads; he said:
With the mangnics and with the amā’im
And the tree al‑āmmah: which reaches the mother of the brain, and it is also the feared one.
He said:
A feared one is buried in its pit, a frost ... the physician poured it like a furnace
Abu Hatim said: a camel is feared: when its back is stripped of bones its hump disappears.
He said:
It is not a feared one nor a reply
Al‑Khalil said: the mother of opposites: its strongest and its farthest.
And the mother of the towns: Mecca; and every city is the mother of all the towns around it, likewise the mother of flesh.
And the mother of the Qur’an: the opening of the Book.
And the mother of the Book: what is on the preserved tablet.
And the mother of the spear: its tip and what is wrapped around it.
He said:
And we will seize the spear in it its mother ... from the hand of the disobedient and what the length endures
And the Arabs say to a woman on whom something descends: mother of a dwelling, and to a man: father of a dwelling.
Ibn al‑ʿArabī says: the mother of Mirzam: the north, he says:
When he becomes evening with the white scarf ... the upper nose is covered by the mother of Mirzam
And the mother of a dog: fever.
In it is the Prophet’s saying, peace be upon him, to Zayd al‑Khail: “A boy will be safe if he escapes from a mother of a dog.”
Likewise the mother of mildam.
And the mother of the stars: the sky.
He said: Taʾabbata Shar‑ran:
He sees the loneliness, the friendly human, and is guided ... where the mother of the stars of the nets guided

Abu Bakr al‑Sunnī reported, al‑Husayn ibn Musabbih from Abu Hanifah said: the mother of the stars: the furnace, because there is no spot in the sky with more stars than it, Taʾabbata Shar‑ran said, and we mentioned the house.
And Dhul‑Rummah said:
With a tuft they stir the filth in their heads ... when the mother of the stars of the nets turns
“turns” means it deviates.
And the mother of Kifāt: the earth.
And the mother of the monkeys, at the back of the wrist above the ankle, and it is where the two monkeys gather like a squirrel.
Abu al‑Najm said:
For the earth from the mother of the black monkeys the low‑lying one
And the mother of the echo is the mother of the brain.
And the mother of ʿUwayf: a spotted duwayba; when it sees a person it rises on its tail and spreads its wings, the proverb is struck with it in cowardice.
He said:
O mother of ʿUwayf, I will spread your two coats ... the emir is standing over you
It is said: it is the locust.
And the mother of ḥumārīs is a black duwayba, many‑legged.
And the mother of ṣabbūr: the confused matter, it is said: it is the ridge that has no opening.
And the mother of ghaylān: a tree full of thorns.
And the mother of al‑luhaym: death.
And the mother of ḥubayn: a beast.
And the mother of the road: most of it.
And the mother of a beast: the triumph, likewise the mother of the gazelle.
He said:
And it fell upon the mother of the gazelle at my need ... if she sends dust on it, the wind blows
And the mother of ṣabbār: the heat.
The brilliant one said:
She defends people from us when we ride her ... from darkness she is called mother of ṣabbār
And the mother of ʿĀmir, and the mother of the road: the hyena.
Yaʿqūb said: the mother of waʿāl: a ridge with an eye.
He said:
And the mother of waʿāl is like this or nearer
And the mother of the palm: the hand.
He said:
It has no finger in the mother of a palm
And the mother of the egg: the ostrich.
Abu Duʿād said:
And I was brought a striving to spread the mother of ... the egg ...
And the mother of ʿĀmir: the triumph.
And the mother of kulayb: a shrub with yellow light.
And the mother of ʿiryiṭ: the scorpion.
And the mother of the lament: the swift.

And the mother of qashʿam, the mother of khashshāf, the mother of the ulcers, the mother of the number, the mother of arayq, the mother of rubayq, the mother of jundab, the mother of al‑baleel, the mother of al‑rubays, the mother of habawkara, the mother of adras, the mother of nād, all are the names of the cunning one.
And the mother of farwah: the ewe.
And the mother of suwayd and the mother of ʿiẓm: the lowest of mankind.
And the mother of jābir: iʿyād.
And the mother of shamlah: the northern cold.
And the mother of ghirs: the rack.
And the mother of khurman: a road.
And the mother of al‑hashīmah: a great tree of dry wood.
Al‑Farazdaq described a pot:
When the mother of al‑hashīmah is fed it boils ... as the mother of the boiled leather boils
And the mother of food: the belly.
He said:
I raised him and he is like a chick; his mother of food sees in his skin a worm
Al‑Khalil said: al‑ummah: religion, Allah the Exalted said: {إِنَّا وَجَدْنَا آبَاءَنَا عَلَى أُمَّةٍ} [الزخرف: 22].
Abu Zayd narrated: He has no nation, i.e. he has no religion.
The Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, said in the story of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl: “A nation will be raised for him alone.”
Likewise anyone who is on a true religion contrary to other religions is a nation.
Every people attributed to something and attached to it are a nation, and every generation of people is a nation up to a limit.
In the hadith: “If it were not that these dogs are a nation among nations I would have ordered their killing, but kill from them every black beast.”
So regarding the verse of Allah: {People were one nation} [Al‑Baqarah: 213], it is said: they were disbelievers, so Allah sent the prophets as bringers of glad tidings and warnings.
And it is said: rather, all those with Noah, peace be upon him, were believers in the ark, then they dispersed.
And it is said: {Indeed Abraham was a nation} [An‑Nahl: 120], i.e. a community led by a guide, and he is the cause of gathering.
The word ummah can also mean a group of scholars, as in the verse of Allah:

{And let there be among you a nation calling to good} [Al‑Imran: 104]; the companion said: ummah = the standing, the Arabs say: “so‑and‑so is tall‑ummah,” meaning the tallness of nations; the poet said:
And indeed Mu‘awiyah al‑akramīn … the handsome faces are the tallness of nations
The Kisa’i said: the nation of a man is his body and his face.
Ibn al‑‘Arabī said: ummah = obedience, and the man is the knowledgeable one.
Abu Zayd said: it is said: indeed he is the handsome of the face‑nation, they attack the Sunnah.
And there is no nation for the sons of so‑and‑so, i.e. they have no face they aim at, but they act like the evening‑time crowd.
Al‑Lihyānī said: how wonderful his nation is, i.e. his creation.
Abu ‘Ubayd said: in language, ‘ummiyy’ is the one to whom the masses are attached and who does not write, i.e. he does not write what he was born with.
And: as for the saying of the poetess:
And does a man of nation, who is obedient, commit a sin?
Then whoever raises him intends a royal law, and whoever makes him broken makes him a religion of adherence, as you said: “Adopt so‑and‑so as a nation.”
And the ummah in the verse of Allah: {And after a nation} [Yusuf: 45], i.e. after a time.
And the imam is anyone who is followed and placed first in affairs.
The Prophet, peace be upon him, is the imam of the imams, the caliph is the imam of the followers, and the Qur’an is the imam of the Muslims.
Al‑Khalil said: immah = blessing.
Al‑‘Asha said:
Your raid struck a nation and removed it.
It is said that the rope on which a building is straightened is called an imam.

Al‑Khalil said: al‑amam = the front, he says: “your chest is before you,” he raised it because it became a name, and says: “your brother is before you,” it is a noun because in the state of attribute it means what is before one’s hands, and as for the saying of Labid:
Thus both breasts think that he … the protector of fear is behind it and before it

Indeed he returned the back and the front to both breasts, as you said: both sides of you are the protector of fear, your right and your left, i.e. its owner and guardian; Abu Zayd said: go rightward, meaning: go before me.
It is said: my right and my left.
He said:
So say: my beloved, I obey you, and listen to my left
And al‑Asma‘ī said: “
Her leader met a nation by her work
” i.e. wherever she turned she found work.
They say: “Before you you see your trace,” i.e. you see what you have presented.
Abu ‘Ubayda said: and among their examples:
Ruwayd: “It will become clear what is in front of you from the Hind”
He says: “It will be established in the matter, do not hurry, it will become clear to you.”
Al‑Khalil said: al‑amam = the easy, insignificant thing, one says: “I did something that is neither great nor low.”
And al‑amam = the close, attainable thing.
He said:
Kufiyyah, a nomad, its place … there is no al‑amam of its house nor its peak
Abu Hatim said: Abu Zayd said: it is said: al‑amam, i.e. small and great, among opposites.
And Ibn Qamī‘ah said about the small:
O my soul, how I lament the youth and … I have not lost it, when I lost it … al‑amam
Al‑Khalil said: al‑amam = the purpose.
Yunus said: this is a blessed matter that people take.
Abu ‘Amrū said: a man is ‘immah, i.e. he declares the land without proof.
He said:
Beware of the answer of the false ‘immah
And Allah, the Exalted, says: {And not those who protect the Sacred House} [Al‑Mā’ida: 2], the plural of “ām” meaning they protect the House of Allah, i.e. they intend it.
Al‑Khalil said: the tayammum runs like the flow of tawakhkh, it is said: “perform tayammum with a good thing and tayammum the best you have and give charity with it.”
And tayammum with the Sa‘īd here means: they took the best and purest thing and used it deliberately.
Thus tayammum became among the masses an act of wiping with Sa‘īd, until they say: “So‑and‑so performed tayammum with dust.”
And Allah, the Exalted, says: {So they performed tayammum with good dust} [An‑Nisā’: 43], i.e. they did it deliberately.
He said:
If my horse were wounded … I rode on an eye and performed tayammum on its owner
And it is said: I performed tayammum with my arrow and spear, i.e. I used it against anyone else, he said:
I performed the spear on Shazr then said to him … this is not a game of the Zaha‑liq
And whoever says in this sense: I performed it, has erred because he said “Shazr” which is only from a side, and he did not mean it in front of him.
Al‑Kisa’i said: the eight‑headed camel is al‑amam.
He said:
May the generous grant me and increase me … an ummah that borders it to me its limits
And the mother: the chief, it is said: he is their mother.
Al‑Shanfara said:
And the mother of children I have witnessed their generosity … when they feed them they become careful and decrease
He meant by mother of children their chief who led them, and it is said: he was extremely wicked
أن: The Khaleel says: you say that a man cries loudly, softly, and with a sigh, and that is his voice in distress.
The Khishash complains and the two streams of cry like ... that the patient goes to his bed.
It is said: a man is very weeping, i.e., he cries a lot.
Al-Lihyan says: it is said: the voice is very weeping: when its sound is long and extended, the poet says:
It is very weeping when it pulls the mouth ... weeping across the sky.
Jacob says: the weeping woman is a woman whose husband dies because of her and she remarries, and whenever she sees him she sings and says: may God have mercy on such-and-such.
And as for the hamza and the haa, they are not a single root, because the stories of sounds are not principles measured upon them, but they say: ahh ahh and aah.
When I go to her at night ... I make the sad man's sigh.
أي: And this is the speaker’s statement:
Unclear or incomplete line – cannot translate accurately.
As for ‘taʾyīt’ and the verse, it has been mentioned in its chapter.
And ‘aa’ – elongated – a tree, and this is his saying:
Unclear or incomplete line – cannot translate accurately.
The friend said: It is said for the story of sounds in the armies and similar: ‘aa’.
Unclear or incomplete line – cannot translate accurately.
And we have said: The sounds in stories are not foundations on which to measure.
بيت: It is said: بيت, بيوت, and أبيات.
And from it is said that the poetic house is called بيت by analogy because it is a collection of words, letters, and meanings, on the specific condition of the meter.
And this is what the speaker meant:
And a بيت on the back of the mat I built... with the brown of the torn khayashim it glitters.
He meant by al‑asmar the pen.
And the بيت: the man's children and those who stay with him.
What a certain person has as a بيت for the night, i.e. what he stays on at night of food and other things.
And he settled the matter when he arranged it at night.
God Almighty said: {إِذْ يُبَيِّتُونَ مَا لَا يَرْضَى مِنَ الْقَوْلِ} [النساء: 108], i.e., when they gather in their houses.
Except that this is specific to the night.
And the بيوات: the water that stays overnight.
And the بيوات: the matter that its owner stays on, being concerned about it.
And I make its poverty a tool... when I fear the بيوات of a matter of hardship (unclear).
And the بيات and the tabyit: to bring the enemy at night, as if you have taken him into his house.
It is narrated from [أَبِي] عُبَيْدَةَ that he said: a thing is بيوت when it is destined, and this is likened to the destiny of poetic بيوت.
And this is not far from the original root that we derived and measured upon.
حمد: It is said: I praised so‑and‑so, I praised him.
And a man named Mahmoud and Muhammad, when his praised qualities are many, they are not blameworthy.
The cripple said: He praised al‑Nu‘man ibn al‑Mundhir, and it is said that he favored him with this word over everyone else he praised that day:
To you, O Abū al‑‘Lan, his speech was ... to al‑Majid, the noble, the generous, al‑Muhammad.
And for this one we mentioned, our Prophet was named Muhammad, peace be upon him and his family.
The Arabs say: may your desire be to do so, i.e., your aim and your deed are praised from you, not blameworthy.
It is said: I praised so‑and‑so when I found him praised, just as one says I was stingy with him when I found him stingy, and I found him incapable.
And this is a rule that is applied to all other attributes.
And I stirred the place when I found it hot, its plant may have withered.
And he stirred the pure gold from the lightning.
If a questioner asks about their saying in the voice of the burning fire of praise; they were told: This is not from that chapter, because it is from the twisted and its root is a bone.
And it has been mentioned in its place.
خط: And from that line which the writer writes.
And from it the line which the potter writes.
God Almighty said: {or a trace of knowledge} [Al-Ahqaf: 4]; they said: it is the line.
It is narrated: “Indeed a prophet among the prophets used to write, so whoever wrote like his writing knew like his knowledge.”
And from the chapter the line of the earth is drawn by a person for himself, because there is an extended trace there.
And from it the line of the dove, and to it the straight arrows are attributed.
And from the chapter the line, and it is the condition; it is said ‘by a line of evil’, because it is a matter that has been drawn for it and upon it.
As for the lined earth, which has not been rained upon between two irrigated lands, it is not from the chapter, and the second ‘ṭā’ is added, because one who errs is as if the rain erred.
The proof of that is the saying of Ibn ‘Abbas: “God made a mistake of its kind”, i.e., when another rain falls it errs, so it does not affect it.
And as for their saying: “On the head of so‑and‑so there is a line”, the people said: it is only a line.
If that is so, it is as if it is a matter that is drawn and has effect, as we have mentioned.
سلم: Scholars say: God, glorified is His praise, is peace; his safety protects creatures from defect, loss, and death.
God, glorified is His majesty, says: {And Allah calls to the abode of peace} [Yunus: 25]; thus peace is God, glorified is His praise, and its abode is Paradise.
Also from this category is Islam, which is submission, because one submits from the father and from abstaining.
And peace: the state of being safe.
And a verb that appears in the verbal noun often related to fighting and combat.
And from the section of companions and submission: the salām called salaf, as if it were a wealth that is given and not withheld from giving.
It may be that the stone was called silām because it is the farthest
thing on earth from decay and disappearance; because of its hardness and solidity.
As for al‑salīm, which is al‑ladiḡ, its naming contains two statements: one that it was submitted because of what it has.
And the other statement is that they exchanged greetings of safety.
And they may name a thing with names of optimism and speculation.
And the ladder (sullam) is known, and it is also from safety; because the one who descends upon it is hoped to have safety.
And safety: a tree, its plural is salām.
And the one that deviated from the door of peace: the dalw which has one branch.
And the salam: a tree, one of its kind is salama.
And the salāmān: a tree.
And from the first category, the silm is reconciliation, and it can be feminine or masculine.
God the Exalted says: {And if they turn to peace, then turn to it} [Al‑Anfal: 61].
And salima: the stone, in which the poet says:
That is my friend and one who reproaches me... he throws behind me with the arrow and the salima.
And the Banu Salima: a group of Ansar not found among the Arabs except them.
And among the names, Salma: a woman.
And Salma: a mountain.
And Abu Sulma, father of Zuhayr, with a doubled sin, is not found among the Arabs except him.
عبد: The first meaning is ‘the servant’, i.e. a slave, and the group is ‘the slaves’; three servants are ‘the worshippers’.
The companion said: except that the masses gathered on the distinction between the servants of God and the enslaved slaves.
This is said of a servant who is a clear example of worship.
We have not heard them use a verb from it; if they had, it would be said ‘abada’, meaning he became a servant and acknowledged worship, but the verb is dead and not used.
He said: as for ‘abada’ meaning to worship, it is said only of one who worships God‑the Exalted.
From him is said ‘abada’ meaning he worships, and ‘ta‘abbada’ meaning he worships intensely.
‘Ta‘abbudan’ (noun) – worship.
Thus ‘al‑mut‘abbid’ is the one who is unique in worship.
And I enslaved so‑and‑so: I took him as a servant.
And as for ‘‘abd’ meaning to serve one’s master, one does not say ‘abada’, nor say he worships his master.
And ‘ta‘abbada’ so‑and‑so, if he makes him like a slave to him even if he is free.
He said:
‘Ta‘abbadani Nimr ibn Sa‘d and I saw … and Nimr ibn Sa‘d is obedient and eager for me.’
It is said: ‘‘abada’ so‑and‑so so‑and‑so’, i.e. he made him a servant.
It is said of the polytheists: ‘the slave‑girl of the tyrant and the idols’; for Muslims: ‘worshippers who worship God‑the Exalted’.
Some of them said: ‘‘abid’ and ‘‘abada’, like servants and servants.”
The feminine of ‘abd’ is ‘‘abda’, just as ‘mamluuk’ and ‘mamluuka’.”
The companion said: ‘al‑‘ibada’: the group of slaves who were born into slavery.”
And from the chapter: ‘the worshipped camel’, i.e. the camel saddled with two loads.”
This also indicates what we said, because that humbles him and lowers him.”
The poet said:
‘Until the whole tribe protected me … and I singled out the lone worshipped camel.’
‘Al‑‘abud’: the humbled one, also used to describe the camel.”
And from the chapter: ‘the worshipped road’, which is the humbled, subjugated one.”
The other root is ‘‘abada’, meaning strength and firmness; it is said ‘this is a garment for him, ‘‘abda’, if he is a strong, sturdy companion.’
And from it comes ‘‘Alqama ibn ‘Abda’, with a fatha on the ba.”
From this analogy ‘‘abd’ is like ‘the nose’ and ‘the heat’.
It is said: ‘He worships this matter.’
It was explained: “Say, if the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first worshipper” (Al‑Zukhruf 81), i.e. the first to be angry about this and to reject his statement.”
It is reported from ‘Ali ‑ peace be upon him ‑ that he said: ‘I worshiped and then was silent’, i.e. I worshiped and then fell silent.”
He said:
‘The ignorant one worships the arrogant by their right … after judgment upon him when there is no worship.’
And another said:
‘I worship that a dog is driven away by the reins.’
It is an expression meaning ‘I am angry about that and I resent it.’
قول: It is said: He said, he says, a statement.
And the spoken thing: the tongue.
And a man of speech and a speaker: one who speaks a lot.
كتب: From that, the book and the writing.
It is said: I wrote the book, I write it as a writing.
And they say: I wrote the mule, when I joined its two ribs with a knot.
He said:
Do not trust a foreigner, you have made it ... upon your palm and write it with bands.
And the writing: the splinter, and it was called that because of its gathered fragments.
And the written: the splinter.
He of al‑Rumma said:
And the overflow of a cavity that exhausted its pits ... a clatter that lost it among the writings.
And from the chapter, the book is the obligation.
God Almighty said: {كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ} [البقرة: 183], and it is said for a ruling: the book.
The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "As for I will judge between you by the Book of God Almighty", meaning his ruling.
And God says: {يَتْلُو صُحُفًا مُطَهَّرَةً} [البينة: 2].
{فِيهَا كُتُبٌ قَيِّمَةٌ} [البينة: 3], i.e., sound judgments.
And it is said for destiny: the book.
Al‑Jaʿdī said:
O daughter of my uncle, the Book of God brought me out ... from you and shall I prevent God what they did.
And from the chapter, the writings of horses, it is said: they wrote.
He said:
With an alif they wrote or a miqnab.
Ibn al‑Aʿrābī said: the writer among the Arabs is the scholar, and he argued with God's saying: {أَمْ عِنْدَهُمُ الْغَيْبُ فَهُمْ يَكْتُبُونَ} [الطور: 41].
And the correspondence: the servant writes to his master on his own.
They said: and its origin is from the book, meaning the condition that is written between them.
لبن: It is said: labintu his milk, al‑binu his milk, when you give milk to it; and so‑and‑so is labin, meaning he has milk, just as one says tamir.
And you deceived me and claimed that you … labin in summer tamir.

Al‑mulbin: great abundance of milk. A she‑camel called labinah is very milky; when its milk falls on its udder it is mulbin, and if it has milk it is labun, a great or thin abundance. A man mulboun is foolish for drinking too much milk. The milk‑fattened horse, the one fed with milk, is preferred. It is said: how much wool of your sheep and its milk, i.e., how many milk‑possessing females it has.

From what deviates from this entry [milk]: neck pain from a pillow, a man is called labin if he has that pain; and from it labinah meaning clay. Ibn al‑Sikkit says it is his brother biliban of his mother, and one does not say bilaban of his mother, only the milk that is drunk. The thing Ibn al‑Sikkit denied is not denied, because it is taken from the drunk milk, as if they were t‑al‑bana laban, as is said … It should be said: it is from the milk, but it is not said bilaban of his mother, rather it is said biliban of his mother.

From what is similar to this milk: the chest, with an open lam. Al‑luban: the khandur, as if it were milk that sweetens from a tree. The analogy is one. From it al‑lubana, which is the need. It may be applied to the entry by a strike of analogy, except that it is nearer to rarity.
